```{r}
# ── Shared statistical helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────
weighted_sd <- function(x, w) {
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(w) & w > 0
  x <- x[keep]
  w <- w[keep]

  if (length(x) < 2L || sum(w) <= 0) return(NA_real_)

  mu <- weighted.mean(x, w)
  sqrt(sum(w * (x - mu)^2) / sum(w))
}

format_mean_sd <- function(mean_value, sd_value) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(mean_value) | is.na(sd_value),
    "—",
    sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", mean_value, sd_value)
  )
}

format_percent <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    "—",
    sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
  )
}

# 95% simulation intervals: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of
# replication-specific estimates (Monte Carlo variation only).
# 95% confidence interval of a survey-weighted NHS estimate. The NHS files
# carry weights but no strata or clusters, so the standard error uses the
# Kish effective sample size, (sum w)^2 / sum(w^2): it allows for unequal
# weights but not for clustering, and so may be somewhat too narrow.
kish_n_eff <- function(w) sum(w)^2 / sum(w^2)
survey_mean_ci <- function(x, w) {
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(w) & w > 0
  x <- x[keep]; w <- w[keep]
  est <- stats::weighted.mean(x, w)
  se <- sqrt(sum(w * (x - est)^2) / sum(w)) / sqrt(kish_n_eff(w))
  c(est = est, lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se)
}
survey_prop_ci <- function(x, w) {
  out <- survey_mean_ci(as.numeric(x), w)
  out[c("lo", "hi")] <- pmin(pmax(out[c("lo", "hi")], 0), 1)
  out
}

q_lo <- function(x) stats::quantile(x, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
q_hi <- function(x) stats::quantile(x, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)

# "mean (lower to upper)"; `scale = 100` turns proportions into percentages.
format_interval <- function(mean, lo, hi, digits = 1, scale = 1) {
  fmt <- function(x) {
    formatC(scale * x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
  }
  dplyr::case_when(
    is.na(mean) ~ "—",
    is.na(lo) | is.na(hi) ~ fmt(mean),
    TRUE ~ paste0(fmt(mean), " (", fmt(lo), " to ", fmt(hi), ")")
  )
}

# ── Shared publication theme ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making: full colour, min 7 pt font.
# Use pub_theme() as the base for every figure; add figure-specific
# theme() overrides (e.g. legend.position) as needed.
pub_theme <- function(base_size = 11) {
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = base_size) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "grey88", linewidth = 0.3),
    strip.background   = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "grey95", colour = NA),
    strip.text         = ggplot2::element_text(size = base_size),
    axis.line          = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "black",  linewidth = 0.4),
    axis.ticks         = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "black",  linewidth = 0.4),
    legend.title       = ggplot2::element_text(size = base_size),
    legend.text        = ggplot2::element_text(size = base_size - 1L),
    legend.key.width   = ggplot2::unit(1.5, "lines")
  )
}
```

## Model Overview

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Model at a glance**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Model name / software** | simeq |
| **Setting** | Portugal (national, adult population) |
| **Perspective** | Population epidemiology and NHS cost perspective |
| **Simulated population** | Adults aged 20–84, initialised from NHS 1998 |
| **Horizon** | 1998–2040 (43 years) |
| **Cycle length** | 1 year |
| **Key outputs** | BMI/obesity trajectories, obesity-attributable QALY loss and years of life lost, high-BMI-attributable direct medical costs |
| **Price year** | Constant 2018 euros; present values in 2026 euros |

:::



### R Package Implementation

simeq is loaded from the local development repository using `devtools::load_all()`. Its core functions prepare model inputs; construct synthetic BMI cohorts; estimate annual BMI transitions; initialise and update the simulated population; apply mortality; add entrant cohorts; calculate QALYs; estimate obesity-attributable costs; and generate validation diagnostics.

Reproducibility is supported by version-controlled source code, fixed random seeds, structured input objects, automated output exports, and this Quarto-based reporting workflow.
This report applies the Portuguese parameter set. The simulation logic is reusable, but transferring the model to another setting requires reassessment of population, BMI-transition, demographic, mortality, utility, and cost inputs.

The analysis was run using the development version of simeq (version `r packageVersion("simeq")`), rendered on `r Sys.Date()`.


### Jurisdictional Transferability

The table below distinguishes components that are generally reusable from those requiring replacement or reassessment when adapting simeq to another jurisdiction.

| Parameter group | Portuguese implementation | Requirement for another jurisdiction |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline population | NHS-based synthetic 1998 adult population | Replace with a local representative baseline population |
| BMI dynamics | Synthetic cohorts from Portuguese NHS waves | Re-estimate using local repeated cross-sectional or longitudinal data |
| Entrant cohorts | NHS donor pools and survey-weight targets | Replace with local entrant distributions and population targets |
| Mortality and demography | Portuguese life table and demographic inputs | Replace with local mortality and demographic data |
| Relative risks | Literature-derived BMI and education mortality RRs | Assess local applicability; use local estimates where possible |
| Utilities | Portuguese EQ-5D-5L age norms and external BMI decrements | Replace or reassess local valuation and utility evidence |
| Costs | Portuguese NHS 2018 direct-cost matrix | Replace with local payer-perspective costs and price year |
| Model logic | Annual individual updating and outcome aggregation | Reusable subject to structural-assumption review |
| Validation routines | Automated comparison framework | Reuse with local targets and predefined criteria |

* * *

## Verification, Validation, and Uncertainty

This section describes the current model-assurance status of the simeq
Portuguese implementation, following the ISPOR–SMDM Reports 1-7 (https://www.ispor.org/heor-resources/good-practices/article/modeling-good-research-practices---overview)


### Current Validation Status

The table below summarises the current assurance status of each model component, using the ISPOR–SMDM distinction between dependent targets used in model development and independent targets not used for that purpose.

The NHS 2005, 2014, and 2019 survey waves contributed to BMI-transition estimation and/or entrant-pool construction. Comparisons with these data are therefore dependent temporal calibration diagnostics rather than independent external validation.

| Component | Empirical target | Used in development? | Classification | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline BMI distribution | NHS 1998 | Yes | Initialisation integrity check | Agreement exact by construction; not predictive |
| Obesity prevalence 2005/2014/2019 | NHS waves | Yes | Dependent temporal calibration | Calibration plot, signed error, MAE and RMSE (@tbl-module1-calibration-metrics) |
| Mortality rates | Portuguese life table | Yes | Internal consistency check | Age–sex death rates vs. life-table input, 1998, 2005, 2014 and 2019 exposure periods, all replications |
| Obesity-attributable QALY loss | No external target | — | Model output | QALY loss from BMI utility decrements (Carrello et al. 2021), with decrement sensitivity analysis; not externally validated |
| Costs | Borges et al. 2018 matrix | Yes | Prevalence-based cost-of-illness | Published 2018 cost matrix rescaled by the simulated high-BMI PAF |
| Independent BMI validation | No withheld source | — | Not yet implemented | Requires a withheld NHS wave or independent survey |



### Uncertainty

Stochastic (first-order, Monte Carlo) uncertainty is quantified using `r n_simulations_main` independent simulation replications with different random seeds. Every interval in this report is a 95% simulation interval: the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replication-specific estimates. These intervals describe Monte Carlo variation only and are not confidence intervals.

Parameter uncertainty is not propagated: the BMI and education mortality relative risks, the BMI-transition coefficients, the GBD relative risks used for PAFs, and the cost inputs are held at their point estimates in every replication. Only the BMI utility decrements have a separate sensitivity analysis (lower and upper bounds of their 95% confidence intervals, @tbl-module2-qaly-decrement-sensitivity).


* * *

## Input Preparation

Model inputs were prepared before simulation and comprise the 1998 baseline population, repeated NHS BMI data, entrant donor pools, and model settings. Mortality uses sex-specific Portuguese life tables for each calendar year from 1998 to 2024 (ages 20–84), projected to 2040 with a Lee-Carter model fitted to 1998–2024 (excluding 2020–2021), and remaining life expectancy from the 2019 table is the reference for years of life lost. The analysis loads this prepared input object and validates its required components before simulation.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-inputs
#| results: hide

report_uncertainty <- TRUE
# Base case: calibrated BMI, i.e. BMI computed after applying the
# self-report correction equations for height and weight (see the BMI calibration section).
# The self-reported (uncorrected) sensitivity analysis uses
# model_inputs_prepared_base_case.rds and runs inside this document (BMI
# calibration section, cached after the first render). Every base-case table and figure,
# including the paper I master results, comes from this one run.
# v10: revision-1 calibration equations (age and region, no education).
prepared_filename <- "model_inputs_prepared_reporting_bias_calibrated_rev1.rds"

data_raw_dir <- file.path(project_root, "data-raw")
prepared_inputs_file <- file.path(data_raw_dir, prepared_filename)
prepare_script_file <- file.path(data_raw_dir, "prepare_model_inputs.R")

if (file.exists(prepared_inputs_file)) {

  # use the cached prepared-inputs file as is

} else if (file.exists(prepare_script_file)) {

  old_wd <- getwd()
  on.exit(setwd(old_wd), add = TRUE)
  setwd(data_raw_dir)

  # The preparation script prints diagnostics; keep them out of the report.
  invisible(utils::capture.output(
    source(
      prepare_script_file,
      local = new.env(parent = globalenv())
    )
  ))

  if (!file.exists(prepared_inputs_file)) {
    stop(
      "`prepare_model_inputs.R` completed but did not create:\n",
      prepared_inputs_file,
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

} else {
  stop(
    "Neither prepared inputs nor a preparation script were found in:\n",
    data_raw_dir,
    "\n\nExpected one of:\n  ", prepared_inputs_file,
    "\n  ", prepare_script_file,
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

inputs <- readRDS(prepared_inputs_file)

required_input_names <- c(
  "population_1998",
  "bmi_panel",
  "life_table",
  "donor_pool_1998",
  "donor_pool_2005",
  "donor_pool_2014",
  "donor_pool_2019",
  "settings"
  # reference_bmi_prevalence is computed below if absent from the inputs file
)

if (!is.list(inputs)) {
  stop(
    "Prepared model inputs must be a named list, but this file contains: ",
    paste(class(inputs), collapse = ", "),
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

missing_inputs <- setdiff(
  required_input_names,
  names(inputs)
)

if (length(missing_inputs) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "Model inputs missing from:\n",
    prepared_inputs_file,
    "\n\nMissing objects:\n",
    paste(missing_inputs, collapse = ", "),
    "\n\nAvailable objects:\n",
    paste(names(inputs), collapse = ", "),
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

population_1998 <- inputs$population_1998
bmi_panel <- inputs$bmi_panel
# Sex-specific Portuguese life tables by calendar year, ages 20-84: observed
# 1998-2024 (built by data-raw/prepare_life_tables.R) and projected
# 2025-2040 with a Lee-Carter model fitted to 1998-2024, excluding 2020-2021
# (mortality_lc/project_life_table_lee_carter_v1.R). The model uses each
# year's table.
life_table_all <- utils::read.csv(
  file.path(project_root, "data", "life_tables", "pt_life_table_model_input_1998_2040_lc.csv")
)
# Last observed life-table year: hybrid mortality calibration is annual up to
# this year and fixed afterwards, while the projected tables set baseline
# mortality from 2025.
last_observed_life_table_year <- 2024L
life_table <- life_table_all[, c("year", "age", "sex", "qx")]

# Remaining life expectancy at each age and sex in 2019, the YLL reference.
ref_life_expectancy <- subset(life_table_all, year == 2019L)[, c("age", "sex", "ex")]
donor_pool_1998 <- inputs$donor_pool_1998
donor_pool_2005 <- inputs$donor_pool_2005
donor_pool_2014 <- inputs$donor_pool_2014
donor_pool_2019 <- inputs$donor_pool_2019
settings_base <- inputs$settings

# reference_bmi_prevalence: use stored value if present, otherwise derive
# from bmi_panel (NHS 2019, Ferreira age bands, non-normal BMI categories).
if ("reference_bmi_prevalence" %in% names(inputs)) {
  reference_bmi_prevalence <- inputs$reference_bmi_prevalence
} else {
  reference_bmi_prevalence <- bmi_panel |>
    dplyr::filter(year == 2019L) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      age_band = dplyr::case_when(
        age <= 29L ~ "20_29",
        age <= 49L ~ "30_49",
        age <= 69L ~ "50_69",
        age <= 84L ~ "70_84"
      ),
      bmi_category = simeq_bmi_category(bmi)
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(age_band), !is.na(bmi_category)) |>
    dplyr::group_by(age_band, bmi_category) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      cat_weight = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    dplyr::group_by(age_band) |>
    dplyr::mutate(prevalence = cat_weight / sum(cat_weight)) |>
    dplyr::ungroup() |>
    dplyr::filter(
      bmi_category %in% c("overweight", "obesity_I", "obesity_II", "obesity_III")
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(age_band, bmi_category, prevalence)
  message("reference_bmi_prevalence computed from bmi_panel (not in inputs file).")
}

message(
  "Loaded prepared model inputs from:\n",
  prepared_inputs_file
)
```

```{r}
#| label: validate-donor-pools

donor_pools <- list(

purrr::walk(
```

## Derived Inputs

Three objects must be constructed before the simulation can run:

- **`rr_bmi`** — all-cause mortality relative risks by BMI category and sex,
  with normal weight as reference. Relative risks are based on the Global BMI
  Mortality Collaboration meta-analysis [@DiAngelantonio2016].

- **`rr_education`** — all-cause mortality relative risks by education level,
  based on the IHME-CHAIN Collaborators meta-analysis [@IHMECHAIN2024].

- **`bmi_transition_model`** — synthetic-cohort BMI-transition model fitted
  from repeated Portuguese NHS cross-sections.

```{r}
#| label: build-rr-bmi

# Global BMI Mortality Collaboration (Di Angelantonio et al., Lancet 2016;
# 388: 776-86), Table 1, primary analysis (never-smokers without chronic
# disease, first 5 years of follow-up excluded), WHO categories with
# 18.5-<25.0 kg/m2 as reference, adjusted for age and sex. The paper reports
# these six-group HRs for both sexes combined, so the same values are used for
# men and women until the sex-specific appendix values are added.
rr_bmi_both_sexes <- tibble::tribble(
  ~bmi_category,    ~rr_bmi,
  "underweight",    1.47,
  "normal_weight",  1.00,
  "overweight",     1.11,
  "obesity_I",      1.44,
  "obesity_II",     1.92,
  "obesity_III",    2.71
)

rr_bmi <- tidyr::crossing(
  sex = c("men", "women"),
  rr_bmi_both_sexes
)
```

```{r}
#| label: build-rr-education

# IHME-CHAIN Collaborators (2024), Lancet Public Health 9: e155-65.
# All-cause adult mortality falls by 1.9% (95% UI 1.8-2.0) per additional
# year of education, with no differential effect by sex: RR = 0.981 per year.
#
# The population has no `education_years` column, so each two-level group
# gets 0.981 ^ (weighted mean years of schooling in that group in 1998).
# Nominal years per three-level category are an assumption (ISCED 0-2 basic
# education, ISCED 3-4 secondary, ISCED 5+ tertiary); change them here.
# Only the ratio between groups matters, because the life-table hazard is
# recalibrated within each age-sex stratum.
rr_education_per_year <- 0.981

nominal_education_years <- c(low = 6, medium = 12, high = 16)

education_years_by_level2 <- population_1998 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    education_years = unname(
      nominal_education_years[as.character(education_level)]
    ),
    education_level2 = dplyr::if_else(
      education_level == "high",
      "higher",
      "lower"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    mean_education_years = stats::weighted.mean(
      education_years,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .by = education_level2
  )

rr_education <- education_years_by_level2 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    education_level2,
    rr_education = rr_education_per_year^mean_education_years
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(match(education_level2, c("lower", "higher")))
```

```{r}
#| label: build-bmi-model

bmi_panel_prepared <- simeq_prepare_bmi_panel(bmi_panel)

bmi_transitions <- simeq_build_bmi_synthetic_cohorts(
  bmi_panel_prepared
)

bmi_transition_model <- simeq_fit_bmi_transition(
  bmi_transitions,
  projection_period = 2014L
)

# Base-case BMI transitions: annual change in each survey-weighted BMI
# percentile (10th to 90th) of each synthetic cohort.
# Earlier-wave respondents are weighted by their probability of surviving
# to the later wave (same mortality model as the simulation), so survivor
# selection is not counted twice; age and period effects differ by sex.
bmi_percentile_model <- simeq_fit_bmi_transition_percentile(
  bmi_panel,
  probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1),
  sex_interactions = TRUE,
  life_table = life_table,
  rr_bmi = rr_bmi,
  rr_education = rr_education
)

# Education after entry: each year some people aged 20-34 with secondary
# education complete higher education. Annual rates by sex and age group come
# from NHS synthetic cohorts and depend on the calendar period of the move
# (the year is the start of the annual cycle, aligned with the entrant pools):
# - moves in 1999-2005 (cycles 1998-2004): the 1998->2005 cohorts;
# - moves in 2006-2014 (cycles 2005-2013): the 2005->2014 cohorts;
# - moves in 2015-2019 (cycles 2014-2018): the 2014->2019 cohorts;
# - moves from 2020 (cycles 2019-2039): set by `education_after_2019`.
# Negative cohort gains give a rate of zero.
#
# `education_after_2019`:
# - "carry_2014_2019": the 2014->2019 rates carried forward to 2040 (base case);
# - "pooled_2005_2019": 2005->2014 and 2014->2019 cohorts pooled, weighted by
#   the geometric mean of the sample sizes;
# - "none": no upgrading after 2019.
education_after_2019 <- "carry_2014_2019"

education_upgrade_1998 <- simeq_fit_education_upgrade(
  bmi_panel,
  periods = 1998L
)
education_upgrade_2005 <- simeq_fit_education_upgrade(
  bmi_panel,
  periods = 2005L
)
education_upgrade_2014 <- simeq_fit_education_upgrade(
  bmi_panel,
  periods = 2014L
)
education_upgrade_post2019 <- switch(
  education_after_2019,
  pooled_2005_2019 = simeq_fit_education_upgrade(
    bmi_panel,
    periods = c(2005L, 2014L)
  ),
  carry_2014_2019 = education_upgrade_2014,
  none = transform(education_upgrade_2014, annual_rate = 0),
  stop("Unknown `education_after_2019`: ", education_after_2019, call. = FALSE)
)
education_upgrade <- simeq_combine_education_upgrade(list(
  list(from = 1998L, to = 2004L, upgrade = education_upgrade_1998),
  list(from = 2005L, to = 2013L, upgrade = education_upgrade_2005),
  list(from = 2014L, to = 2018L, upgrade = education_upgrade_2014),
  list(from = 2019L, to = NA, upgrade = education_upgrade_post2019)
))

# Caption of the upgrade-rate table (built here: chunk options cannot hold
# a long R expression with colons).
education_upgrade_caption <- paste0(
  "Annual probability of moving from secondary (medium) to higher ",
  "education, by period of the move, sex and age group. 1999–2005: NHS ",
  "synthetic cohorts 1998→2005; 2006–2014: 2005→2014; 2015–2019: ",
  "2014→2019; ",
  switch(
    education_after_2019,
    pooled_2005_2019 = "from 2020: 2005→2014 and 2014→2019, pooled.",
    carry_2014_2019 = "from 2020: 2014→2019 carried forward.",
    none = "from 2020: no upgrading."
  )
)
```

## BMI-Transition Model

### Synthetic-cohort construction

Repeated Portuguese NHS cross-sectional survey waves from 1998, 2005, 2014,
and 2019 were used to construct synthetic cohorts. Because the NHS waves do not
follow the same respondents longitudinally, the synthetic cohorts represent
population groups with shared stable characteristics rather than observed
individual-level trajectories. BMI change is therefore inferred at the
synthetic-cohort level, not from individual follow-up data.

Synthetic cohorts were defined by **sex** (men, women), **education level**
(higher, lower), and **five-year age group at the baseline survey wave**
(12 groups: 20–24, 25–29, ..., 75–79 years). This gives 2 × 2 × 12 = 48
cohorts per transition interval.

Three consecutive survey-wave pairs were used, producing 144 synthetic
transitions in total:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi-transition-intervals
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Synthetic-cohort transition intervals used to estimate annual BMI change. Each interval contributes 48 cohorts (2 sex × 2 education × 12 five-year age groups, 20–79)."

bmi_transitions |>
  dplyr::distinct(year_t, year_t1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(interval_years = year_t1 - year_t, n_cohorts = 48L) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year_t) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::cols_label(
    year_t = "Earlier NHS wave", year_t1 = "Later NHS wave",
    interval_years = "Interval (years)", n_cohorts = "Cohorts"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns = c(year_t, year_t1), use_seps = FALSE) |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns = c(interval_years, n_cohorts)) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(100), table.font.size = 11)
```

Each cohort is followed to the same birth cohort at the later wave, with ages shifted by the exact interval between the waves (7, 9 or 5 years). For each cohort, survey-weighted BMI percentiles (10th to 90th) are computed at both waves, and the annual change in percentile $p$ for cohort $c$ is:

$$
\Delta\mathrm{BMI}_{\mathrm{annual},\,c,\,p}
= \frac{Q_{c,\,t_1}(p) - Q_{c,\,t_0}(p)}{t_1 - t_0}
$$

where $Q_{c,t}(p)$ is the weighted $p$-th percentile of BMI in cohort $c$ at wave $t$. Modelling each percentile separately lets the upper part of the BMI distribution rise faster than the median, as observed in the NHS waves.

### BMI updating in the simulation

For each percentile, the annual change is regressed on sex, age, age², education and survey period, weighted by the geometric mean of the two waves' weighted cohort sizes.

In each annual simulation cycle, each survivor's rank within their sex × education × five-year age group is computed from the current survey-weighted BMI distribution. The survivor receives the predicted change interpolated at that rank; ranks below the 10th or above the 90th percentile take the change at that percentile. BMI is retained as a continuous variable and recategorised after each update for obesity-prevalence, mortality-risk, utility, and cost calculations. Values are constrained to a plausible range of 10–80 kg/m² after each cycle. [https://github.com/NCD-RisC/Data-cleaning-protocol/blob/main/README.md]

The later wave of each synthetic cohort contains only survivors, and people with higher BMI die sooner, so the raw change between waves mixes BMI change with survivor selection. Because the simulation applies BMI-specific mortality separately, using the raw change would count that selection twice. Each earlier-wave respondent is therefore weighted by their probability of surviving the interval under the simulation's own mortality model (life-table hazard rescaled within sex and five-year age group, times the BMI and education relative risks, with BMI held at its earlier-wave value) before the earlier-wave percentiles are computed. The age, age-squared and survey-period terms are allowed to differ by sex.

Each survey period's estimates apply to the years it covers: 1998–2004, 2005–2013, and 2014 onwards. The 2014–2019 estimates are held constant after 2019. This stationarity assumption is structural and will be examined in scenario analyses.



### BMI measurement

BMI in the Portuguese NHS is derived from self-reported height and weight. The base case corrects for self-report bias by applying sex-specific calibration equations with age and region to height and weight before BMI is computed (@sec-bmi-calibration).

**Sensitivity analysis.** The model is re-run with uncorrected self-reported BMI to show how much the correction changes the results.


### NHS wave characteristics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi-transition-waves
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Portuguese NHS waves used for synthetic-cohort BMI-transition estimation, restricted to respondents aged 20–84 with valid BMI and survey weight."

bmi_panel |>
  dplyr::filter(year %in% c(1998L, 2005L, 2014L, 2019L)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    survey_records      = dplyr::n(),
    weighted_population = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi            = weighted.mean(bmi, w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = year
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::cols_label(
    year = "NHS wave", survey_records = "Survey records",
    weighted_population = "Weighted population",
    mean_bmi = gt::html("Weighted mean BMI (kg/m²)")
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns = year, use_seps = FALSE) |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns = c(survey_records, weighted_population)) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = mean_bmi, decimals = 2) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(100), table.font.size = 11)

```

### Education classification: three-level reporting versus binary transition model

The simulation population retains a three-level education variable for output
reporting: `low`, `medium`, and `high`. The BMI-transition model requires a
binary grouping: `education_level2`. The mapping is:

- **`low` and `medium`** → `lower` (used in BMI-transition estimation)
- **`high`** → `higher` (used in BMI-transition estimation)

Consequently, individuals with `low` and `medium` education receive identical
BMI-transition predictions; only the `high`-versus-`low`/`medium` contrast
is captured by the transition model. Separate transition estimates for `low`
and `medium` education would require sufficient sample sizes in the NHS waves
to sustain the additional grouping.

Entrants take the education of NHS respondents aged 20–24, but many people complete higher education after age 20. @tbl-higher-education-by-wave shows this: within a wave, the share with higher education (more than 12 years) is larger at ages 30–34 than at 20–24 for women, and the same birth cohorts gain higher education between waves. Keeping education fixed from entry would therefore understate the share with higher education in every later year (in test runs, about 15% of men and 20% of women in 2019, against 20% and 25% in the NHS).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-higher-education-by-wave
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Weighted share of adults with higher education (more than 12 years of schooling) at ages 20–24 and 30–34, by sex and NHS wave. Source: NHS BMI panel, survey-weighted."

higher_education_by_wave <- bmi_panel |>
  dplyr::filter(age >= 20L, age <= 34L) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_group = dplyr::case_when(
      age <= 24L ~ "20–24",
      age >= 30L ~ "30–34",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(age_group)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_records = dplyr::n(),
    share_higher_education = stats::weighted.mean(
      education_level == "high",
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .by = c(year, sex, age_group)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year, sex, age_group)

write_result_csv(
  higher_education_by_wave,
  "supplement_higher_education_by_wave_age_sex.csv"
)

higher_education_by_wave |>
  dplyr::mutate(sex = dplyr::recode(sex, women = "Women", men = "Men")) |>
  dplyr::select(year, sex, age_group, share_higher_education) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = age_group, values_from = share_higher_education) |>
  gt::gt(groupname_col = "year") |>
  gt::cols_label(sex = "Sex") |>
  gt::tab_spanner(label = "Share with higher education", columns = c(`20–24`, `30–34`)) |>
  gt::fmt_percent(columns = c(`20–24`, `30–34`), decimals = 1) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(100), table.font.size = 11,
                  row_group.font.weight = "bold")
```

The model therefore lets education change after entry. Each year, a person aged 20–34 with `medium` (secondary) education moves to `high` education with an annual probability that depends on sex and five-year age group (@tbl-education-upgrade-rates). The move happens after the BMI update, so it affects the person's BMI transitions and mortality from the next year onward. Rates are estimated from synthetic cohorts: for each pair of waves and each baseline age group, the gain in the cohort's weighted share with higher education is divided by the years between waves and by the baseline share with secondary education. The rates depend on the calendar period of the move. Moves in 1999–2005 use the 1998→2005 cohorts, moves in 2006–2014 the 2005→2014 cohorts and moves in 2015–2019 the 2014→2019 cohorts. Where the cohort share with higher education fell between two waves, the rate is zero (women in 1998→2005; both sexes at ages 25–34 in 2014→2019). `r switch(education_after_2019, pooled_2005_2019 = "From 2020, rates are pooled over the 2005→2014 and 2014→2019 cohorts (weighted by the geometric mean of the two sample sizes).", carry_2014_2019 = "From 2020, the 2014→2019 rates are carried forward.", none = "No upgrading is applied from 2020.")` Movement from `low` education, and any change after age 34, is not modelled.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-education-upgrade-rates
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: !expr education_upgrade_caption

write_result_csv(
  as.data.frame(education_upgrade),
  "education_upgrade_rates.csv"
)

as.data.frame(education_upgrade) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    period = factor(
      dplyr::case_when(
        year_min == 1998 ~ "1999–2005",
        year_min == 2005 ~ "2006–2014",
        year_min == 2014 ~ "2015–2019",
        TRUE ~ "From 2020"
      ),
      levels = c("1999–2005", "2006–2014", "2015–2019", "From 2020")
    ),
    sex = dplyr::recode(sex, women = "Women", men = "Men"),
    age_group = paste0(age_min, "–", age_max),
    annual_rate
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = annual_rate) |>
  gt::gt(groupname_col = "period") |>
  gt::cols_label(age_group = "Age group") |>
  gt::tab_spanner(label = "Annual probability", columns = c(Women, Men)) |>
  gt::fmt_percent(columns = c(Women, Men), decimals = 2) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(60), table.font.size = 11)
```

### BMI-transition handling for ages 80–84

Synthetic cohorts are defined for baseline age groups 20–24 through 75–79. The follow-up of the 75–79 group lands in the 80–84 stratum, which is observed in the data. Ages 80–84 cannot serve as a *baseline* because their follow-up would require survey data for ages 87+, which do not exist. Annual BMI change for individuals aged 80–84 in the simulation is therefore obtained by extrapolating the fitted quadratic age function beyond its observed range. The weighted ordinary least-squares transition model includes a quadratic age term:

$$\Delta\mathrm{BMI} \sim \mathrm{sex} + \mathrm{age} + \mathrm{age}^2 + \mathrm{education} + \mathrm{period}$$

- BMI transitions for ages 80–84 are extrapolated from the fitted quadratic age function beyond the observed 20–79-year baseline range.

### Annual event sequence

The following sequence is applied in each simulation year (transitioning the
state from year $t$ to year $t+1$):

1. **Mortality** — death probability assigned from life-table hazard × BMI and
   education RRs; deaths drawn stochastically and recorded with year $= t+1$.
2. **BMI updating** — survivors' BMI updated by the predicted annual change at
   their percentile rank within their cohort group; BMI constrained to 10–80 kg/m².
3. **Demographic updating** — survivors aged by one year; people who turn 85 leave the model;
   calendar year advanced to $t+1$.
4. **Entrant generation** — age-20 entrants sampled from the period-appropriate
   donor pool, assigned year $= t+1$; survivors and entrants combined.

The simulation stores annual demographic and health states for each individual. Costs and QALYs are calculated subsequently by applying the relevant cost and utility inputs to these records.

### Key assumptions

- Repeated NHS cross-sections support synthetic-cohort estimates of population-level BMI change; they do not observe individual BMI trajectories.
- Synthetic cohorts are defined by sex, binary education level, and five-year baseline age group; these characteristics are treated as stable across survey waves.
- BMI transitions differ by BMI percentile within each synthetic cohort, so people higher in their cohort's BMI distribution can gain more.
- The base case assumes that the 2014–2019 BMI-transition estimates remain constant after 2019.
- BMI transitions for ages 80–84 are extrapolated from the fitted quadratic age term, because no synthetic cohort has an 80–84 baseline.
- Uncertainty in the BMI-transition parameters, mortality relative risks, and cost inputs is not propagated; the 95% simulation intervals reflect Monte Carlo variation only. @sec-cost-rr-sensitivity shows how the costs change across the 95% uncertainty intervals of the GBD relative risks.

* * *

## Module 1: Obesity Trajectories 1998–2040

The simulation is initialised in 1998 using the full NHS baseline population aged 20–84 years. From 1999 onwards, new age-20 entrants are sampled from period-specific donor pools. Comparisons with NHS data from 2005, 2014, and 2019 are reported as dependent temporal calibration diagnostics because these waves contributed to transition estimation and entrant-pool construction.

### Simulation Settings

```{r}
#| label: settings-module1

settings_historical <- simeq_settings(
  initial_year = 1998L,
  projection_end_year = 2040L,
  entry_age = 20L,
  max_age = 84L,
  n_simulations = n_simulations_main,
  entrant_n_per_year = 100L,
  seed = 20260817L
)
```



### Entrant Targets

Entrants are assigned the weighted age-20 NHS population size from the survey wave nearest to their entry year. The model uses the 1998 wave for entry years 1999–2004, the 2005 wave for 2005–2013, the 2014 wave for 2014–2018, and the 2019 wave for 2019–2040.

```{r}
#| label: entrant-targets-module1

entrant_by_wave <- bmi_panel |>
  filter(age == 20L, year %in% c(1998L, 2005L, 2014L, 2019L)) |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(
    entrant_population = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  rename(wave_year = year)

entry_years <- seq.int(
  settings_historical$initial_year + 1L,
  settings_historical$projection_end_year
)

entrant_targets_historical <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  entry_year = entry_years,
  sex = c("men", "women")
) |>
  mutate(
    wave_year = case_when(
      entry_year <= 2004L ~ 1998L,
      entry_year <= 2013L ~ 2005L,
      entry_year <= 2018L ~ 2014L,
      TRUE ~ 2019L
    )
  ) |>
  left_join(entrant_by_wave, by = c("wave_year", "sex")) |>
  select(entry_year, sex, entrant_population) |>
  mutate(
    entry_year = as.integer(entry_year),
    entrant_population = as.numeric(entrant_population)
  ) |>
  arrange(entry_year, sex)

if (anyNA(entrant_targets_historical$entrant_population)) {
  stop(
    "Entrant targets are missing. Check bmi_panel includes age == 20 in all NHS waves.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

simeq_validate_entrant_targets(
  entrant_targets = entrant_targets_historical,
  start_year = settings_historical$initial_year + 1L,
  end_year = settings_historical$projection_end_year
)

write_result_csv(entrant_targets_historical, "module1_entrant_targets.csv")
```

### Simulation

Simulation outputs are stored as versioned RDS files in `analysis/results/`. Increment `simulation_version` whenever changes to model inputs, parameters, or simulation logic affect results. The full person-year microsimulation trace is kept only as RDS (compressed, versioned); a CSV of that scale would be redundant with the RDS and impractical to store. Summary tables derived from it are exported as CSV throughout this document.

```{r}
#| label: run-module1
#| cache: false

donor_pools_module1 <- list(
  list(from = 1999L, to = 2004L, pool = donor_pool_1998),
  list(from = 2005L, to = 2013L, pool = donor_pool_2005),
  list(from = 2014L, to = 2018L, pool = donor_pool_2014),
  list(from = 2019L, to = 2040L, pool = donor_pool_2019)
)

sim_path <- file.path(results_dir, sim_rds)

if (file.exists(sim_path)) {
  simulation_historical <- readRDS(sim_path)

  cached_simulations <- dplyr::n_distinct(simulation_historical$simulation)
  if (cached_simulations != n_simulations_main) {
    stop(
      "Cached simulation has ", cached_simulations,
      " simulation(s), but n_simulations_main is ", n_simulations_main,
      ". Delete the stale cache or increment simulation_version.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
} else {
  simulation_historical <- simeq_run_simulation(
    population = population_1998,
    settings = settings_historical,
    life_table = life_table,
    last_observed_year = last_observed_life_table_year,
    rr_bmi = rr_bmi,
    rr_education = rr_education,
    donor_pool = donor_pool_1998,
    donor_pools = donor_pools_module1,
    entrant_targets = entrant_targets_historical,
    # Unused by the percentile method; kept so the call matches the legacy one.
    bmi_transition_model = bmi_transition_model,
    bmi_update_method = "percentile",
    bmi_percentile_model = bmi_percentile_model,
    bmi_period = "by_year",
    stochastic_bmi = TRUE,
    education_source = "existing",
    bmi_limits = c(10, 80),
    education_upgrade = education_upgrade
  )

  save_result_rds(simulation_historical, sim_rds)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: computational-performance
#| echo: false
#| include: true

# ── Computational-environment metadata ───────────────────────────────────────
# Recorded for reproducibility documentation (R version, package version,
# git commit, OS, hardware). Hardware detection is cross-platform: it tries
# each OS's native source and falls back to "Not available" rather than
# relying on Windows-only `wmic` calls, which return nothing on Linux/macOS
# render environments (e.g. CI, this GitHub Pages build).

pkg_version <- as.character(utils::packageVersion("simeq"))
git_commit  <- tryCatch(
  system("git rev-parse --short HEAD", intern = TRUE, ignore.stderr = TRUE),
  error = function(e) "unknown"
)
r_version <- paste0(R.version$major, ".", R.version$minor)
os_string <- paste(Sys.info()[["sysname"]], Sys.info()[["release"]])

get_cpu_name <- function() {
  sysname <- Sys.info()[["sysname"]]
  tryCatch(
    {
      if (sysname == "Linux") {
        info <- readLines("/proc/cpuinfo", warn = FALSE)
        line <- grep("^model name", info, value = TRUE)[1]
        if (is.na(line)) return("Not available")
        trimws(sub("^model name\\s*:\\s*", "", line))
      } else if (sysname == "Darwin") {
        trimws(system("sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string", intern = TRUE))
      } else if (sysname == "Windows") {
        out <- system("wmic cpu get name /value", intern = TRUE, ignore.stderr = TRUE)
        trimws(sub("Name=", "", grep("Name=", out, value = TRUE)[1]))
      } else {
        "Not available"
      }
    },
    error = function(e) "Not available"
  )
}

get_total_ram_gb <- function() {
  sysname <- Sys.info()[["sysname"]]
  tryCatch(
    {
      if (sysname == "Linux") {
        info <- readLines("/proc/meminfo", warn = FALSE)
        kb <- as.numeric(sub("\\D", "", grep("^MemTotal", info, value = TRUE)))
        round(kb / 1024^2, 0)
      } else if (sysname == "Darwin") {
        bytes <- as.numeric(system("sysctl -n hw.memsize", intern = TRUE))
        round(bytes / 1024^3, 0)
      } else if (sysname == "Windows") {
        out <- system(
          "wmic computersystem get TotalPhysicalMemory /value",
          intern = TRUE, ignore.stderr = TRUE
        )
        bytes <- as.numeric(sub("TotalPhysicalMemory=", "", grep("TotalPhysicalMemory=", out, value = TRUE)))
        round(bytes / 1024^3, 0)
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }
    },
    error = function(e) NA_real_
  )
}

cpu_name <- get_cpu_name()
ram_gb   <- get_total_ram_gb()

# Simulation dataset metrics
n_people          <- dplyr::n_distinct(simulation_historical$person_id)
n_replications    <- dplyr::n_distinct(simulation_historical$simulation)
n_years           <- dplyr::n_distinct(simulation_historical$year)
n_record_years    <- nrow(simulation_historical)
ram_sim_mb        <- round(as.numeric(object.size(simulation_historical)) / 1024^2, 0)

# Runtime is recorded when the simulation runs; if loaded from cache the
# elapsed time below reflects I/O only.
sim_rds_info      <- file.info(file.path(results_dir, sim_rds))
sim_size_mb       <- round(sim_rds_info$size / 1024^2, 0)

computational_performance <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Metric,                             ~Value,
  "simeq package version",             pkg_version,
  "Git commit",                        git_commit,
  "R version",                         R.version$version.string,
  "Operating system",                  os_string,
  "CPU",                               cpu_name,
  "Total RAM",                         if (is.na(ram_gb)) "Not available" else paste0(ram_gb, " GB"),
  "Initial cohort size (1998)",        format(n_people, big.mark = ","),
  "Simulation replications",           as.character(n_replications),
  "Simulation years",                  paste0(n_years, " (1998–2040)"),
  "Total person-year records",         format(n_record_years, big.mark = ","),
  "Simulation output size (on disk)",  paste0(sim_size_mb, " MB"),
  "Simulation output size (RAM)",      paste0(ram_sim_mb, " MB")
)

write_result_csv(computational_performance, "module1_computational_performance.csv")

computational_performance |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::cols_label(Metric = "Metric", Value = "Value") |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    gt::md("Hardware fields fall back to \"Not available\" when the render
           environment does not expose them (e.g. some containers/CI runners).")
  ) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(100), table.font.size = 11)
```

```{r}
#| label: verify-baseline-identity
#| include: false

baseline_identity <- simulation_historical |>
  dplyr::filter(
    simulation == 1L,
    year == settings_historical$initial_year,
    alive
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    person_id,
    age_simulated = age,
    sex_simulated = sex,
    education_level_simulated = education_level,
    education_level2_simulated = education_level2,
    bmi_simulated = bmi,
    survey_weight_simulated = survey_weight,
    height_simulated = height,
    weight_simulated = weight
  ) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    population_1998 |>
      dplyr::select(
        person_id,
        age_input = age,
        sex_input = sex,
        education_level_input = education_level,
        education_level2_input = education_level2,
        bmi_input = bmi,
        survey_weight_input = survey_weight,
        height_input = height,
        weight_input = weight
      ),
    by = "person_id",
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    bmi_difference = bmi_simulated - bmi_input,
    survey_weight_difference = survey_weight_simulated - survey_weight_input,
    height_difference = height_simulated - height_input,
    weight_difference = weight_simulated - weight_input,
    age_matches = age_simulated == age_input,
    sex_matches = sex_simulated == sex_input,
    education_matches = education_level_simulated == education_level_input,
    education2_matches = education_level2_simulated == education_level2_input
  )

baseline_identity_summary <- baseline_identity |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_baseline_input = nrow(population_1998),
    n_matched = dplyr::n(),
    n_unmatched = n_baseline_input - n_matched,
    max_abs_bmi_difference = max(abs(bmi_difference), na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi_difference = mean(bmi_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_abs_weight_difference = max(abs(weight_difference), na.rm = TRUE),
    max_abs_height_difference = max(abs(height_difference), na.rm = TRUE),
    max_abs_survey_weight_difference = max(
      abs(survey_weight_difference),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    all_age_match = all(age_matches),
    all_sex_match = all(sex_matches),
    all_education_match = all(education_matches),
    all_education2_match = all(education2_matches)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: summarise-module1
#| include: false

# ── One combined pass over the living population ──────────────────────────────
# data.table is 5-15x faster than dplyr for large grouped operations.
# The function works on a filtered copy, so simulation_historical stays in
# memory for modules 2 and 3. The self-reported BMI sensitivity run
# (BMI calibration section) is summarised with the same function.

summarise_living_population <- function(simulation_output) {
  sim_dt <- data.table::as.data.table(simulation_output)[alive == TRUE]
  sim_dt[, obesity    := bmi >= 30L]
  sim_dt[, overweight := bmi >= 25L & bmi < 30L]

  # Step 1: per-replication weighted means (one pass over the data)
  by_rep_dt <- sim_dt[,
    .(
      mean_bmi               = sum(bmi        * survey_weight) / sum(survey_weight),
      obesity_prevalence     = sum(obesity    * survey_weight) / sum(survey_weight),
      overweight_prevalence  = sum(overweight * survey_weight) / sum(survey_weight),
      weighted_population    = sum(survey_weight),
      n_records              = .N
    ),
    by = .(simulation, year, sex, education_level)
  ]

  # Step 2: across-replication summary — intervals for BMI and obesity prevalence
  living_summary <- by_rep_dt[,
    .(
      bmi_lo                   = quantile(mean_bmi,           0.025),
      bmi_hi                   = quantile(mean_bmi,           0.975),
      mean_bmi                 = mean(mean_bmi),
      obesity_prevalence_lo    = quantile(obesity_prevalence,    0.025),
      obesity_prevalence_hi    = quantile(obesity_prevalence,    0.975),
      obesity_prevalence       = mean(obesity_prevalence),
      overweight_prevalence_lo = quantile(overweight_prevalence, 0.025),
      overweight_prevalence_hi = quantile(overweight_prevalence, 0.975),
      overweight_prevalence    = mean(overweight_prevalence),
      weighted_population      = mean(weighted_population),
      n_records                = mean(n_records)
    ),
    by = .(year, sex, education_level)
  ] |>
    tibble::as_tibble() |>
    dplyr::arrange(year, sex, education_level) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      sex             = factor(sex,             levels = c("women", "men")),
      education_level = factor(education_level, levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
    )

  list(by_rep = tibble::as_tibble(by_rep_dt), summary = living_summary)
}

module1_living <- summarise_living_population(simulation_historical)

# bmi_by_rep (per replication) is reused by later tables.
bmi_by_rep <- module1_living$by_rep
historical_living_summary <- module1_living$summary

rm(module1_living)
invisible(gc())

write_result_csv(
  historical_living_summary,
  "module1_living_population_summary.csv"
)
```

### Mortality Input Consistency Check

> **Classification:** Internal consistency check. The Portuguese life table is an input to the simulation; this comparison therefore assesses whether simulated mortality is consistent with the input structure rather than providing independent validation. Differences reflect BMI and education relative-risk adjustment and stochastic variation. Results should be reassessed across repeated simulation runs before drawing conclusions.

```{r}
#| label: mortality-consistency-check
#| include: false

age_breaks_mx <- c(20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 85)
age_labels_mx <- c("20–29", "30–39", "40–49", "50–59", "60–69", "70–79", "80–84")

# Exposure years: the population alive at the start of year t and the deaths
# recorded in year t + 1 (the t to t + 1 transition), one per NHS wave.
mx_exposure_years <- c(1998L, 2005L, 2014L, 2019L)

add_age_band_mx <- function(data) {
  data |>
    mutate(
      age_band = cut(
        age,
        breaks = age_breaks_mx,
        right = FALSE,
        labels = age_labels_mx
      )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(age_band))
}

lt_mx <- life_table |>
  filter(year %in% mx_exposure_years) |>
  mutate(mx_per1000 = -log1p(-qx) * 1000) |>
  add_age_band_mx() |>
  group_by(year, sex, age_band) |>
  summarise(
    lt_mx_per1000 = mean(mx_per1000, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sim_denom_mx <- simulation_historical |>
  filter(year %in% mx_exposure_years, alive) |>
  add_age_band_mx() |>
  group_by(year, simulation, sex, age_band) |>
  summarise(
    population_weight = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sim_numer_mx <- simulation_historical |>
  filter(year %in% (mx_exposure_years + 1L), !alive) |>
  add_age_band_mx() |>
  mutate(year = year - 1L) |>
  group_by(year, simulation, sex, age_band) |>
  summarise(
    death_weight = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Death rate within each replication, then mean and 95% simulation interval.
sim_mx <- sim_denom_mx |>
  left_join(sim_numer_mx, by = c("year", "simulation", "sex", "age_band")) |>
  mutate(
    death_weight = replace_na(death_weight, 0),
    sim_mx_per1000 = 1000 * death_weight / population_weight
  ) |>
  group_by(year, sex, age_band) |>
  summarise(
    sim_mx_lo = q_lo(sim_mx_per1000),
    sim_mx_hi = q_hi(sim_mx_per1000),
    sim_mx_per1000 = mean(sim_mx_per1000),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mortality_consistency <- lt_mx |>
  left_join(sim_mx, by = c("year", "sex", "age_band")) |>
  mutate(
    exposure_period = paste0(year, "/", year + 1L),
    mx_ratio = sim_mx_per1000 / lt_mx_per1000,
    mx_abs_diff = sim_mx_per1000 - lt_mx_per1000
  )

write_result_csv(
  mortality_consistency,
  "module1_mortality_consistency.csv"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mortality-consistency
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Mortality input consistency: life-table central death rate versus simulated death rate for the 1998/1999, 2005/2006, 2014/2015 and 2019/2020 exposure periods, by sex and age group. For each period, the population alive at the start of the first year is followed to deaths recorded in the second year. Simulated rates are the mean across replications (95% simulation interval). Differences reflect relative-risk adjustment and stochastic variation."

mortality_consistency |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex = factor(
      dplyr::recode(sex, women = "Women", men = "Men"),
      levels = c("Women", "Men")
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(sex, year, age_band) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    group = paste0(sex, ", ", exposure_period),
    sim_mx_ci = format_interval(sim_mx_per1000, sim_mx_lo, sim_mx_hi, digits = 2)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(group, age_band, lt_mx_per1000, sim_mx_ci, mx_ratio, mx_abs_diff) |>
  gt::gt(groupname_col = "group") |>
  gt::cols_label(
    age_band       = "Age band",
    lt_mx_per1000  = gt::html("Life-table mₓ (per 1,000)"),
    sim_mx_ci      = gt::html("Simulated mₓ (per 1,000), mean (95% SI)"),
    mx_ratio       = "Ratio (sim / LT)",
    mx_abs_diff    = "Difference (per 1,000)"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = c(lt_mx_per1000, mx_abs_diff), decimals = 2) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = mx_ratio, decimals = 3) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(100), table.font.size = 11,
                  row_group.font.weight = "bold")
```

### Stochastic Stability

Across `r n_simulations_main` independent stochastic replications, selected population-level outcomes showed limited first-order stochastic variation. Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSEs) and coefficients of variation (CVs) were calculated from the distribution of replication-specific, survey-weighted outcome estimates. MCSEs quantify the precision of the mean model estimate across replications, whereas CVs describe the relative variation in outcome estimates between replications.

```{r}
#| label: module1-stochastic-stability
#| include: false

stability_years <- reported_years

stochastic_outputs <- simulation_historical |>
  dplyr::filter(
    alive,
    year %in% stability_years
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, simulation) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    mean_bmi = weighted.mean(
      bmi,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    obesity_prevalence = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 30,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stochastic_stability <- stochastic_outputs |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_bmi, obesity_prevalence),
    names_to = "outcome",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, outcome) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_replications = dplyr::n_distinct(simulation),
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_between_replications = sd(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    mcse = sd_between_replications / sqrt(n_replications),
    cv_pct = 100 * sd_between_replications / mean_estimate,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    mcse_display = dplyr::if_else(
      outcome == "obesity_prevalence",
      100 * mcse,
      mcse
    )
  )

if (any(stochastic_stability$n_replications != n_simulations_main)) {
  stop(
    "Expected ", n_simulations_main, " replications in every year, found ",
    paste(unique(stochastic_stability$n_replications), collapse = ", "),
    ". Check dev_mode and the cached simulation file.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

write_result_csv(
  stochastic_stability,
  "module1_stochastic_stability.csv"
)
```

### Retrospective Calibration

Simulated obesity prevalence was compared with observed NHS prevalence in 2005, 2014, and 2019, separately by sex. These comparisons represent dependent temporal calibration diagnostics because the corresponding NHS waves contributed to BMI-transition estimation and/or entrant-pool construction. Simulated estimates are reported as the mean across independent stochastic replications, with empirical 2.5th–97.5th percentile intervals showing variation across replications.

```{r}
#| label: module1-retrospective-calibration
#| include: false

validation_years <- c(2005L, 2014L, 2019L)

observed_prevalence <- bmi_panel |>
  dplyr::filter(year %in% validation_years) |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, sex) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(bmi)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    obesity_prevalence_observed = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 30,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    obs_lo = survey_prop_ci(bmi >= 30, survey_weight)[["lo"]],
    obs_hi = survey_prop_ci(bmi >= 30, survey_weight)[["hi"]],
    n_observed = dplyr::n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

simulated_prevalence_by_replication <- simulation_historical |>
  dplyr::filter(
    alive,
    year %in% validation_years
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, sex, simulation) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    obesity_prevalence = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 30,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

simulated_prevalence <- simulated_prevalence_by_replication |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, sex) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    obesity_prevalence_simulated = mean(
      obesity_prevalence,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    sim_lo = quantile(
      obesity_prevalence,
      probs = 0.025,
      na.rm = TRUE,
      names = FALSE
    ),
    sim_hi = quantile(
      obesity_prevalence,
      probs = 0.975,
      na.rm = TRUE,
      names = FALSE
    ),
    n_simulations = dplyr::n_distinct(simulation),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

validation_combined <- simulated_prevalence |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    observed_prevalence |>
      dplyr::select(
        year,
        sex,
        obesity_prevalence_observed,
        obs_lo,
        obs_hi,
        n_observed
      ),
    by = c("year", "sex")
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year, sex)

validation_errors <- validation_combined |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    signed_error = obesity_prevalence_simulated -
      obesity_prevalence_observed,
    absolute_error = abs(signed_error)
  )

mae <- mean(validation_errors$absolute_error, na.rm = TRUE)

rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(validation_errors$signed_error^2, na.rm = TRUE)
)

write_result_csv(
  validation_combined,
  "module1_validation_prevalence.csv"
)

write_result_csv(
  validation_errors,
  "module1_validation_errors.csv"
)
```


```{r}
#| label: tbl-module1-validation
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Dependent temporal calibration: simulated and observed NHS obesity prevalence at survey years, by sex."

validation_table <- validation_combined |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex = dplyr::recode(
      sex,
      women = "Women",
      men = "Men"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    sex,
    simulated = format_interval(
      obesity_prevalence_simulated, sim_lo, sim_hi, scale = 100
    ),
    observed = format_interval(
      obesity_prevalence_observed, obs_lo, obs_hi, scale = 100
    )
  )

validation_table |>
  gt::gt(groupname_col = "year") |>
  gt::cols_label(
    sex = "Sex",
    simulated = "Simulated, % (95% SI)",
    observed = "Observed NHS, % (95% CI)"
  ) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(
    font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")
  ) |>
  gt::tab_options(
    table.width = gt::pct(100),
    table.font.size = 11,
    row_group.font.weight = "bold"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = gt::md(
      "Simulated estimates are means across independent stochastic replications; the 95% simulation interval (SI) is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile across replications and describes run-to-run stochastic variation. Observed NHS estimates are survey-weighted; the 95% confidence interval (CI) uses the Kish effective sample size, which allows for unequal weights but not for the survey's clustering, so it may be somewhat too narrow."
    )
  )
```

### Calibration Error Metrics

Across the six sex-by-year comparisons, simulated obesity prevalence increased over time but was lower than observed NHS prevalence in every comparison. Mean absolute error and root mean squared error were calculated from differences between the mean simulated and observed prevalence estimates.

The percentile method lets the upper part of the BMI distribution rise faster than the median, as observed, and the survivor weighting described in the BMI-transition section removes the double counting of selective mortality. Simulated obesity nevertheless remains below the calibrated NHS values in 2005–2019 (in development runs, by about 1.6 percentage points for men and 2.7 for women in 2019), with mean BMI about 0.2–0.3 kg/m² below. Letting education rise after entry widens the gap slightly (by about 0.3–0.6 percentage points), because more people follow the smaller BMI gains of the higher-education group; the education structure itself now matches the NHS (@tbl-education-validation). The gap is concentrated at ages 50–64. Part of it reflects the simulated age structure: the model has no migration and adds people only at age 20, so it holds fewer adults aged 65–84 than the NHS weights, and older adults have higher obesity. The rest reflects population change that the closed synthetic cohorts do not represent. The 2025 wave (@sec-validation-2025) gives an independent check of the projection.

### Out-of-sample Validation: NHS 2025 {#sec-validation-2025}

The 2025 NHS wave was not used to estimate BMI transitions, build entrant pools or set any other model input, so it gives an independent check of the projection six years after the last wave used in fitting. It was cleaned with `data-raw/prepare_nhs_2025_validation.R`, which applies the same filters and self-report calibration equations as the earlier waves. Observed values below use calibrated BMI, as in the base case.

```{r}
#| label: module1-validation-2025
#| include: false
#| cache: false

validation_2025_file <- file.path(data_raw_dir, "nhs_2025_validation_rev1.rds")
validation_2025_available <- file.exists(validation_2025_file) &&
  2025L %in% simulation_historical$year

if (validation_2025_available) {
  nhs_2025_validation <- readRDS(validation_2025_file)

  add_all_adults <- function(data) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(data, dplyr::mutate(data, sex = "all"))
  }

  observed_2025 <- nhs_2025_validation |>
    add_all_adults() |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      n_observed = dplyr::n(),
      bmi_observed = stats::weighted.mean(bmi, survey_weight),
      bmi_observed_lo = survey_mean_ci(bmi, survey_weight)[["lo"]],
      bmi_observed_hi = survey_mean_ci(bmi, survey_weight)[["hi"]],
      obesity_observed = stats::weighted.mean(bmi >= 30, survey_weight),
      obesity_observed_lo = survey_prop_ci(bmi >= 30, survey_weight)[["lo"]],
      obesity_observed_hi = survey_prop_ci(bmi >= 30, survey_weight)[["hi"]],
      obesity_self_reported = stats::weighted.mean(
        bmi_self_reported >= 30, survey_weight
      ),
      .by = sex
    )

  simulated_2025 <- simulation_historical |>
    dplyr::filter(alive, year == 2025L) |>
    add_all_adults() |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      mean_bmi = stats::weighted.mean(bmi, survey_weight),
      obesity = stats::weighted.mean(bmi >= 30, survey_weight),
      .by = c(simulation, sex)
    ) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      bmi_simulated = mean(mean_bmi),
      bmi_lo = q_lo(mean_bmi),
      bmi_hi = q_hi(mean_bmi),
      obesity_simulated = mean(obesity),
      obesity_lo = q_lo(obesity),
      obesity_hi = q_hi(obesity),
      .by = sex
    )

  validation_2025 <- dplyr::left_join(simulated_2025, observed_2025, by = "sex") |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      obesity_difference = obesity_simulated - obesity_observed,
      obesity_ratio = obesity_simulated / obesity_observed,
      sex = factor(sex, levels = c("women", "men", "all"))
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(sex)

  write_result_csv(validation_2025, "module1_validation_nhs2025.csv")
}
```

#### Education structure

@tbl-education-validation compares the simulated share with higher education with the NHS, by sex and age group. NHS 1998, 2005, 2014 and 2019 were used to estimate the upgrade rates; 2025 was not.

```{r}
#| label: education-validation
#| include: false

education_observed <- bmi_panel |>
  dplyr::filter(year %in% c(2005L, 2014L, 2019L))

if (exists("nhs_2025_validation")) {
  education_observed <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    education_observed,
    dplyr::select(nhs_2025_validation, year, sex, age, education_level, survey_weight)
  )
}

education_age_group <- function(age) {
  as.character(cut(
    age,
    breaks = c(19, 34, 49, 64, Inf),
    labels = c("20–34", "35–49", "50–64", "65–84")
  ))
}

add_all_ages <- function(data) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(data, dplyr::mutate(data, age_group = "20–84"))
}

education_validation_observed <- education_observed |>
  dplyr::filter(age >= 20L, age <= 84L) |>
  dplyr::mutate(age_group = education_age_group(age)) |>
  add_all_ages() |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    observed = stats::weighted.mean(education_level == "high", survey_weight),
    .by = c(year, sex, age_group)
  )

education_validation <- simulation_historical |>
  dplyr::filter(alive, year %in% unique(education_validation_observed$year)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(age_group = education_age_group(age)) |>
  add_all_ages() |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    share = stats::weighted.mean(education_level == "high", survey_weight),
    .by = c(simulation, year, sex, age_group)
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    simulated = mean(share),
    simulated_lo = q_lo(share),
    simulated_hi = q_hi(share),
    .by = c(year, sex, age_group)
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(education_validation_observed, by = c("year", "sex", "age_group")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    year, sex,
    factor(age_group, levels = c("20–34", "35–49", "50–64", "65–84", "20–84"))
  )

write_result_csv(education_validation, "module1_validation_education.csv")
```

```{r}
                  row_group.font.weight = "bold")
```

### BMI Calibration and Self-Reported BMI Sensitivity Analysis {#sec-bmi-calibration}

#### Rationale

BMI in the Portuguese NHS is computed from self-reported height and weight. Self-report introduces systematic measurement error: individuals tend to over-report height and under-report weight, with the direction and magnitude of bias varying by sex, age and region of residence. Left uncorrected, this produces downward bias in mean BMI and obesity prevalence estimates, and may differentially affect subgroups. The base case therefore uses calibrated BMI, derived by applying sex-specific correction equations with age and region to height and weight before BMI is computed. The sensitivity analysis uses uncorrected self-reported BMI instead.

All other model inputs, parameters, and simulation settings are identical in the two runs. The calibration is applied during data preparation, so in the base case it propagates through the full simulation — initial population, BMI-transition panel, and entrant donor pools all use calibrated BMI.

#### Calibration model

Two ordinary least squares models are estimated separately by sex: one regressing measured height (cm) on self-reported height, and one regressing measured weight (kg) on self-reported weight. Both models adjust for age (years) and region of residence (seven Portuguese NUTS regions; North as reference). Education is not included: adding it did not improve out-of-sample performance (calibration paper, revision 1, Supplementary Tables S7-S9).

For height:

$$
\hat{h}_{\text{calib}} = \alpha_h + \beta_h \cdot h_{\text{SR}} + \beta_{h,\text{age}} \cdot \text{age} + \gamma_{h,\text{region}}
$$

For weight:

$$
\hat{w}_{\text{calib}} = \alpha_w + \beta_w \cdot w_{\text{SR}} + \beta_{w,\text{age}} \cdot \text{age} + \gamma_{w,\text{region}}
$$

Calibrated BMI is then computed as:

$$
\text{BMI}_{\text{calib}} = \frac{\hat{w}_{\text{calib}}}{\left(\hat{h}_{\text{calib}} \,/\, 100\right)^2}
$$

#### Coefficients (Table S6)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-calibration-coefficients
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Table S6. Calibration coefficients for self-reported height (cm) and weight (kg) by sex. North is the reference category. The coefficient on the self-reported measurement is the slope relating self-reported to measured values; all other terms are additive adjustments."

calibration_coefs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~term,                         ~height_women,          ~height_men,           ~weight_women,          ~weight_men,
  "Intercept",                   "20.945",               "15.480",              "−0.670",               "−2.260",
  "Self-reported value (slope)", "0.871",                "0.913",               "1.014",                "1.018",
  "Age (per year)",              "−0.061",               "−0.031",              "0.010",                "0.036",
  "Region: North",               "Ref.",                 "Ref.",                "Ref.",                 "Ref.",
  "Region: Center",              "0.433",                "−0.065",              "0.080",                "−0.725",
  "Region: Lisbon M.A.",         "0.699",                "−0.214",              "0.121",                "−0.540",
  "Region: Alentejo",            "0.372",                "−0.484",              "−0.541",               "−0.848",
  "Region: Algarve",             "1.131",                "0.183",               "−0.143",               "0.230",
  "Region: Madeira",             "0.977",                "−0.053",              "0.171",                "−0.436",
  "Region: Azores",              "0.373",                "−0.135",              "0.002",                "−0.036"
)

calibration_coefs |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_spanner(label = "Height (cm)", columns = c(height_women, height_men)) |>
  gt::tab_spanner(label = "Weight (kg)", columns = c(weight_women, weight_men)) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    term         = "Term",
    height_women = "Women", height_men = "Men",
    weight_women = "Women", weight_men = "Men"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_style(
    style     = gt::cell_text(style = "italic"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = grepl("^Ref\\.", height_women))
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    gt::md("Reference category: North region. Calibration paper, revision 1, Supplementary Table S9.
           Slopes are dimensionless ratios of measured to self-reported values.")
  ) |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(100), table.font.size = 11)
```

The height slope is below 1.0 for both sexes (0.871 for women, 0.913 for men), confirming that over-reporting of height is attenuated toward the population mean: taller individuals tend to over-report by less. The weight slope is close to 1.0 for both sexes (1.014 and 1.018), indicating near-proportional under-reporting. Regional effects on height are larger for women than men; weight adjustments show larger regional variation in men.

#### Results

The self-reported scenario is simulated in this document with the same settings, seed and replications as the base case, using the uncorrected inputs `data-raw/model_inputs_prepared_base_case.rds`. It runs on the first render and is cached afterwards. If those inputs are missing, the results below are skipped.

```{r}
#| label: load-sensitivity-results
#| include: false
#| cache: false

# Self-reported BMI sensitivity run. It uses the uncorrected inputs written
# by data-raw/prepare_model_inputs.R with apply_reporting_bias_calibration =
# FALSE (model_inputs_prepared_base_case.rds) and otherwise the same
# settings, seed, life tables, mortality RRs, entrant targets and percentile
# BMI transitions as the base case. The simulation runs once; its summary is
# cached next to the base-case simulation, so later renders only read it.
# Delete the cache file if the inputs or the model change.
sensitivity_summary_file <- file.path(
  results_dir,
  paste0(
    "sensitivity_self_reported_living_summary_",
    simulation_version, "_nsim", n_simulations_main, ".rds"
  )
)

self_reported_candidates <- file.path(
  data_raw_dir,
  c("model_inputs_prepared_base_case.rds",
    "model_inputs_prepared_self_reported.rds")
)
self_reported_inputs_file <- self_reported_candidates[
  file.exists(self_reported_candidates)
][1]

if (file.exists(sensitivity_summary_file)) {

  sensitivity_living_summary <- readRDS(sensitivity_summary_file)

} else if (!is.na(self_reported_inputs_file)) {

  self_reported_inputs <- readRDS(self_reported_inputs_file)

  self_reported_percentile_model <- simeq_fit_bmi_transition_percentile(
    self_reported_inputs$bmi_panel,
    probs = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1),
    sex_interactions = TRUE,
    life_table = life_table,
    rr_bmi = rr_bmi,
    rr_education = rr_education
  )

  self_reported_simulation <- simeq_run_simulation(
    population = self_reported_inputs$population_1998,
    settings = settings_historical,
    life_table = life_table,
    last_observed_year = last_observed_life_table_year,
    rr_bmi = rr_bmi,
    rr_education = rr_education,
    donor_pool = self_reported_inputs$donor_pool_1998,
    donor_pools = list(
      list(from = 1999L, to = 2004L, pool = self_reported_inputs$donor_pool_1998),
      list(from = 2005L, to = 2013L, pool = self_reported_inputs$donor_pool_2005),
      list(from = 2014L, to = 2018L, pool = self_reported_inputs$donor_pool_2014),
      list(from = 2019L, to = 2040L, pool = self_reported_inputs$donor_pool_2019)
    ),
    entrant_targets = entrant_targets_historical,
    # Unused by the percentile method; kept so the call matches the base case.
    bmi_transition_model = bmi_transition_model,
    bmi_update_method = "percentile",
    bmi_percentile_model = self_reported_percentile_model,
    bmi_period = "by_year",
    stochastic_bmi = TRUE,
    education_source = "existing",
    bmi_limits = c(10, 80),
    education_upgrade = education_upgrade
  )

  # Person-level run, used by the fixed-budget application's self-reported
  # sensitivity analysis (bmi_source = "self_reported").
  save_result_rds(
    self_reported_simulation,
    sub("_nsim", "_self_reported_nsim", sim_rds, fixed = TRUE)
  )

  sensitivity_living_summary <- summarise_living_population(
    self_reported_simulation
  )$summary

  saveRDS(sensitivity_living_summary, sensitivity_summary_file)

  rm(self_reported_simulation, self_reported_inputs)
  invisible(gc())

} else {
  message(
    "Self-reported BMI inputs not found. Expected one of:\n  ",
    paste(self_reported_candidates, collapse = "\n  "),
    "\nRun data-raw/prepare_model_inputs.R with ",
    "apply_reporting_bias_calibration <- FALSE to create them."
  )
}

sensitivity_available <- exists("sensitivity_living_summary")
```

## Module 2: Quality-adjusted Life Years

### Population-weighted QALYs {#sec-qaly}

QALYs are calculated for simulated individuals who are alive using age-specific Portuguese EQ-5D-5L utility norms [@Ferreira2023]. The population norms already include people with overweight and obesity, so they are first back-calculated to a healthy-weight baseline: within each age band, the prevalence-weighted BMI decrements (from the 2019 NHS BMI distribution) are added back to the norm. An education-specific shift from the same norms is added, and the BMI-related utility decrements [@Carrello2021] are then applied to individuals with BMI ≥25 kg/m². No decrement is applied to underweight BMI because the selected evidence covers overweight and obesity only.

The module reports the mean annual QALY per person (total survey-weighted QALYs divided by survey-weighted person-years, with deaths counting half a year). These values are not estimates of education-related QALY inequality or externally validated measures of disease burden.

The end of @sec-qaly reports the QALY loss attributable to obesity and to high BMI. @sec-yll reports obesity-attributable years of life lost (YLL). PAFs are computed using obesity classes I–III as the exposed categories (BMI ≥ 30), with all-cause mortality relative risks from the Global BMI Mortality Collaboration [@DiAngelantonio2016]; overweight and underweight contribute zero to the PAF. DALYs are not reported, because a disability component built from the BMI utility decrements would duplicate the QALY loss. This is a population-level approximation; it is not a disease-specific implementation comparable to the GBD or to Borges et al. (2025).

```{r}
#| label: run-module2-qalys
#| cache: false

qaly_results <- simeq_calculate_qalys(
  simulation_output = simulation_historical,
  min_age = 20L,
  max_age = 84L,
  reference_bmi_prevalence = reference_bmi_prevalence
)

if (!"by_year" %in% names(qaly_results)) {
  stop(
    "`simeq_calculate_qalys()` must return an object named `by_year`.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}


write_result_csv(
  qaly_results$by_year,
  "module2_qalys_by_year.csv"
)

if ("overall" %in% names(qaly_results)) {
  write_result_csv(
    qaly_results$overall,
    "module2_qalys_overall.csv"
  )
}

# Decedents contribute half a year (half_cycle_deaths = TRUE), so the
# per-person mean divides total QALYs by weighted person-years, not by the
# population alive at the end of the cycle.
qaly_results_per_person <- qaly_results$by_year |>
  dplyr::group_by(year) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    weighted_population_alive = sum(
      mean_weighted_population,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    weighted_person_years = sum(
      mean_weighted_person_years,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    total_qalys_weighted = sum(
      mean_total_qalys_weighted,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    mean_qaly_per_person = dplyr::if_else(
      weighted_person_years > 0,
      total_qalys_weighted / weighted_person_years,
      NA_real_
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

write_result_csv(
  qaly_results_per_person,
  "module2_qalys_per_person_by_year.csv"
)

# Replication-specific QALY per person, for 95% simulation intervals.
qaly_per_person_by_sim <- qaly_results$individual |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    qaly_per_person = sum(qaly_weighted) / sum(survey_weight * person_years),
    .by = c(simulation, year)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-module2-qalys-overall
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Mean annual QALY per person in the simulated adult population, 1998–2040. Mean across simulation replications (95% simulation interval)."

qaly_per_person_by_sim |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    mean_1998_2040 = mean(qaly_per_person, na.rm = TRUE),
    qaly_1998      = qaly_per_person[year == 1998L],
    qaly_2019      = qaly_per_person[year == 2019L],
    qaly_2040      = qaly_per_person[year == 2040L],
    change         = qaly_2040 - qaly_1998,
    .by = simulation
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-simulation, names_to = "measure") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    value = format_interval(mean(value), q_lo(value), q_hi(value), digits = 4),
    .by = measure
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    measure = dplyr::recode(
      measure,
      mean_1998_2040 = "Mean annual QALY per person, 1998–2040",
      qaly_1998      = "QALY per person, 1998",
      qaly_2019      = "QALY per person, 2019",
      qaly_2040      = "QALY per person, 2040",
      change         = "Absolute change, 1998–2040"
    )
  ) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::cols_label(measure = "", value = "Mean (95% simulation interval)") |>
  gt::opt_stylize(style = 1, color = "gray") |>
  gt::opt_table_font(font = gt::google_font("Source Sans Pro")) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.width = gt::pct(100), table.font.size = 11)
```
